decision.explanation: For an eigenvector (x,y) corresponding to λ=-5+3i, the first row gives (3-3i)x-3y=0, so y=(1-i)x. The columns of P are the real and imaginary parts of a complex eigenvector (up to sign), hence a²+b²=|x|² and c²+d²=|y|²=2|x|². The requested ratio is 1/2.

$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda =-5+3\text{i},$ and that $A=PC{P}^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5+3\text{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-5+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-5+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -5+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3-3\text{i} & -3 \\ 6 & -3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(3-3\text{i}){x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}+(-3-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(1-\text{i}){x}_{1}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1-\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}\text{i}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1+2\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}\text{i}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1+2\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda =1+2\text{i},$ and that $A=PC{P}^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda =1+2\text{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-2\text{i} & 2 \\ -4 & -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-2\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-2-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-1+\text{i}){x}_{1}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-1+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

and v is an eigenvector of A corresponding to the complex eigenvalue λ.

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(2−2i)x1+2x2=0−4x1+(−2−2i)x2=0.

Since the matrix A−λI is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

Hence, the general solution is given by

[x1(−1+i)x1],x1∈C.

content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda =1+2\text{i},$ and that $A=PC{P}^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda =1+2\text{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-2\text{i} & 2 \\ -4 & -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-2\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-2-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-1+\text{i}){x}_{1}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-1+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

after.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2-3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1+3\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}-2-3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2-2\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=2+2\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ -5-8\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -5 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

v=[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 8\text{i}-5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2-2\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=2+2\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ -5-8\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -5 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
